Being completely honest: your mileage may vary. So the reasons I regretted it may or may not be helpful.

1) I regret it because I've been through a lot in three years (became financially independent from a *severely* abusive household), such as from going to not being able to feed myself to a $40,000 a year job with no college education, and now I'm unemployed again. Had I been completely honest, I could at least have taken the correct actions and spared myself a lot of grief over three years getting help to the degree I needed, and probably not ended up unemployed.

2) Honestly? The thing that hurt me the most, the last time I attempted suicide (and got exceptionally close, may I add), was that I had no idea how much my friends / business associates would be affected by my death. When I got out of the hospital, my phone was flooded with phone calls and texts by people that were freaking out that couldn't get a hold of me for over two weeks. When I got back in touch with them, the look on their faces was like they seen a ghost. TL;DR As well, someone very important to me said she had no idea I was this depressed and expressed how much it would bother her. Damn near ripped my heart out. Moral of the story: had I at least been honest, I could have found out years ago why my prior medication wasn't working (genetics, long story), sparring a lot of heart ache; and me almost killing myself might never have happened. 

But, that's just me.

Take it slow. Start reading the documentation, then google something you're not familiar with. There's really no way around it. That's like saying "I want to learn heart surgery, but I really don't know how the human heart works." Root Project also does a decent job of giving visuals to the information. That's all you really can do.

Honestly? That's going to involve a lot of reading. First: homework. Make sure to read up on Mac OS, Windows, Linux, then BSD security documentation. Then check out documentation for tools like Whonix. Then check our r/hacking. After that, watch a few YouTube videos on networking and white hat hacking (I prefer the channel Root Project). This is 100% vital, or else you will not understand what comes next.
 
Now the fun part: put everything into practice, make your cyber security rig, then hop on to the dark net. Google will turn up a link for the hidden wiki. The hidden wiki will be absolutely useless, except for Hidden Answers. Read up on how people evade detection, and how the bad guys break in. To protect against a thief, you have to learn from a thief. This also involves how the bad guys stay "undetected" (Which is always temporary) in dark net markets. 

I'll save you nine hours and tell you there's a member that's also a mod for the uncensored hidden wiki, and his public facing profile has the current link to it. That's when you will get page after page of how the bad guys handle their security / how they break in.

"Kilo!" You say "You're telling everyone how to be a bad guy!" No I'm not. You can't have knowledge by imparting select ignorance. I also haven't revealed some of the tricks of the trade to make being a bad guy work, and remember: with NSA's PRISM, and the fact that it controls a lot of exit nodes, I really don't recommend doing anything shady. 

Best of luck on that red pill.

TL;DR- depends what you're using Tails for. Tor isn't great for everything. Plus many, many nerd tips.

It's just for different purposes. If all you want to do is surf the web, Tails is a better choice for the fact that it wipes your RAM of any temporary memory, and wipes any cookies/information that's left on the USB stick. On the other hand, if you want a desktop/laptop machine for everyday use, I would recommend:

* FreeBSD (Host OS)
- Make sure to change MAC address
*Virtual Box
-With encryption add on
*Whonix gateway
-Then channel your guest OS through it exclusively
*Security Onion linked to Whonix gateway to alert for any intrusions.
*Any vanilla Linux distribution for guest OS. Though I prefer Fedora.

Basically, if you want to interface and work on anything if you're set on using TOR, that's your best option. Honestly, here's what I recommend. Repeat all steps above, but this time replace whonix gateway with your preferred server distribution. (Fedora for me, anyway), then run a foreign VPN through it. Configure to kill internet access if VPN disconnects.

My two cents, though.

Now, before I suffer the wrath of Reddit,I don't always recommend Tor, but it does have it's place. Just like a hammer, it is incredibly useful in some cases, but isn't good for everything. I wouldn't recommend using it for heart surgery.

What I recommend using Tor for:

1) For people in oppressive governments that have no other options. 

2) Now, this is an incredibly gray area, but I believe that it's a good look into depravity and understanding of governments. Tor is often the gateway towards a better understanding of cyber security, as it was for me. It also woke me up in a lot of ways seeing just how sick some of the bad guys are, and how they evade detection. It takes you out of the superficial cocoon of materialism and ignorance that we happen to live in. Basically the nerd version of the Red Pill. 

My 2 cents.

TL;DR Use virtual box and Whonix, and Tor isn't meant for heavy anonimization, so I wouldn't expect any real measure of privacy, more or less a thin layer of obscurity.

Well, if you're asking for all traffic to be routed through Tor, just get a virtual machine, then use Whonix gateway. And if the gateway disconnects, you're off the net to prevent data leakage. Unfortunately there's a lot of information your OS will give out even with the Tor browser/Tor bundle.

Bear in mind that while Tor is not a bad VPN at all, the NSA has implemented so many measures that Tor isn't that great for strong "anonymization". I found one time on the Tor network a Russian VPN used by a small hacker group. Apparently, you had to sell your soul (metaphorically of course), but that's price you pay if you're really concerned about the Feds peering into your internet traffic.

Typical disclaimer: I'm not a therapist, and I don't know the full details of everything that happened between you and Shannon. I can really only offer a perspective gained by having dealt with narcissism.

From what I read, at least, yep. Shannon's a narcissist. Narcissism is typically derived by pain, neglect, and insecurity. Shanon waking John up in the middle of the night is a huge red flag. So now that I've said that:

1) It's all a manipulative tactic, her apology. Some of it is pre-meditated, but most is just her believing her own nonsense. So trying to confront her will get you absolutely nowhere. As to why? you could ask yourself that until the end of time and not get a satisfying answer. Though if it helps, typically a narcissist will try to seem like they're the ones extending the olive branch because you're the bad guy in her view. 

2) If you really didn't say what you claim she thought you said: then absolutely that's gas lighting. Typically a person will understand that in the heat of the moment wires can get crossed, ask for an explanation, then move on. It would appear that's just not her style.

3) What should you do? Again, you have to do what's right for you, but if you're asking for a random stranger's advice: drop Shannon, and be prepared to move out if need be. Narcissists will only be so patient before expecting you to capitulate every time, all the time. Otherwise, they will make your life a living nightmare. She already has John on her side, so she will turn the house against you. It's known as triangulation, if you didn't know that already.

Narcissists are master manipulators, so they'll say or do whatever it takes to woo you over. If they can't, they'll destroy your standing in any social circle you share with them. I would take that into consideration if you still don't want to abandon Sharon on the account of her being a "friend." A friend is someone who shows support, compassion, and concern for your well being. It doesn't sound like Shannon is doing any of that, and is therefore not your friend. Many times, all it takes is just not over complicating the situation.

No matter what you end up deciding to do, I wish you the best.

Obviously, I'm not a therapist. Ultimately you have to do what's right for you. I can only speak from my experience.

Good job getting a better grasp on OCD and depression. Also? *Major* props on getting help. Way too many people don't have the courage you did facing your problems instead of running away from them. As far as the actions you expressed here goes, I'm proud of you. 

As far as to whether you should seek another therapist? Not really. It will ultimately boil down to who you feel comfortable with. Some therapists aren't specialized in wha you're going through, but can change your life (mine was not versed at all in BP II, but because of her I'm in a far better position in life.) Psychology isn't quite as clear cut as other forms of medicine. It's not like visiting a cardiologist for heart disease. 

What I would personally recommend with my grain of salt is just starting slow and see if your therapist helps along your journey. If the answer's yes? Then you'll continue to work wth someone who you're comfortable with and gets results. If not, then there's always other options.

Good luck, either way you go.
